summary: Defines how to convert contact information between JSContact and vCard. It gives conversion rules for every JSContact and vCard element registered with IANA at publication time, and defines new properties and parameters so unknown or custom elements can still be converted. It updates RFC 6350.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a translation guide between two ways of writing address cards, with a plan for words that neither side has seen before.

questions: how to convert vcard to jscontact
subtitle: Rules for converting contact cards between the JSContact (JSON) and vCard formats, including data neither side has a place for.

tldr.problem: JSContact is meant as an alternative to vCard and jCard, but applications that prefer JSContact still have to talk to services and clients that only understand vCard or jCard, and the reverse.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives conversion rules for every JSContact and vCard element registered with IANA at the time of publication. For anything with no registered counterpart, it defines the JSContact properties vCardProps, vCardParams and vCardName, the vCard property JSPROP and the vCard parameters JSCOMPS and JSPTR.
tldr.outcome: A card can be converted in either direction, and unknown or custom elements can survive the round trip. The RFC updates RFC 6350.

today: RFC 9555 is a Proposed Standard and updates RFC 6350. It has been updated by RFC 9982, so read that document alongside it.

sections.title: Why a Conversion Specification
sections.content:
The JSContact data model and format (RFC 9553) aims to be an alternative to the widely used vCard standard (RFC 6350) and the jCard format (RFC 7095). Applications that prefer JSContact are still likely to interoperate with services and clients that support only vCard or jCard. Existing vCard or jCard users may also want to represent their data in JSContact.

This document therefore defines standard rules for converting contact data between JSContact and vCard, and so also jCard. Its vCard-to-JSContact section follows the structure of vCard v4, and it also covers properties and parameters from vCard extension RFCs, including the ones in RFC 9554.
sections.plainLanguage: Two groups write down people's contact details in different styles. This guide lets them swap cards without mistakes.

sections.title: General Rules and Value Types
sections.content:
The vCard UID property is optional, but a JSContact Card must have a uid. An implementation that converts a vCard without a UID MUST generate a unique identifier. It SHOULD give the same value when the same vCard is converted again, though how is implementation-specific.

Multivalued JSContact properties are JSON objects keyed by an Id. Without a PROP-ID parameter, an implementation may choose any key, but it MUST generate values that are valid for the Id type in RFC 9553.

Value types map as follows: TEXT, URI and LANGUAGE-TAG become JSContact String (URIs must follow RFC 3986, language tags RFC 5646), BOOLEAN becomes Boolean, FLOAT becomes Number, and INTEGER becomes Int or UnsignedInt. TIMESTAMP becomes UTCDateTime, except in anniversaries where it becomes a Timestamp. A DATE becomes a PartialDate for an anniversary unless it holds only a month or only a day. TIME, DATE-TIME and DATE-AND-OR-TIME have no JSContact counterpart and are handled by the extension properties described below.
sections.plainLanguage: Before translating the details, the guide says how to translate plain things like words, numbers and dates, and what to do when a card has no ID number.

sections.title: How vCard Parameters Convert
sections.content:
Many vCard parameters turn into a property of the converted JSContact object. PREF becomes pref, MEDIATYPE becomes mediaType, SORT-AS becomes sortAs and PROP-ID becomes the Id key of the object. TYPE becomes either contexts or kind, and by default the vCard values home and work become the JSContact contexts private and work.

LEVEL becomes the level of a PersonalInfo object. On EXPERTISE, the values beginner, average and expert convert to low, medium and high. ALTID has no registered JSContact counterpart, but several rules use it to combine several vCard properties into a single JSContact object.

The LANGUAGE parameter turns into an entry in the Card's localizations property, keyed by the language tag. The RFC defines no single rule for building the patch values and gives two options: one patch per property, or bundling patches by parent. Localizations only localize properties that are present in the non-localized Card. The GROUP parameter does not convert, because it is for jCard only and MUST NOT be set in a vCard.
sections.plainLanguage: Little notes attached to a detail, such as 'this is my work phone' or 'this one is preferred', each have a matching spot on the other side. The guide lists which spot.

sections.title: How vCard Properties Convert
sections.content:
Each vCard property maps to an object in a named Card property. For example, N becomes the Name object, ADR becomes an Address in addresses, TEL becomes a Phone in phones, EMAIL an EmailAddress in emails, ORG an Organization, TITLE and ROLE a Title, and NOTE a Note. FN becomes the Name's full property. BDAY, DEATHDATE and ANNIVERSARY become Anniversary objects whose kind is birth, death or wedding.

Structured values convert component by component. Each component of N and ADR becomes a NameComponent or AddressComponent with a kind. Backwards-compatible components need care. For N, a value that also appears in the secondary surname or generation component is ignored when it appears again in the family name or honorific suffix. For ADR, the extended address and street address components are ignored if the value uses the newer format from RFC 9554.

The TEL TYPE values cell, fax, main-number, pager, text, textphone, video and voice become Phone features (with cell becoming mobile). An implementation SHOULD set features only if the TEL has a TEL-specific TYPE. ADR, GEO and TZ are independent in vCard but all map to an Address object, and the properties MUST be converted to the same address when their GROUP values match, or when GROUP is unset on them but set on other ADR, GEO or TZ properties.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of card line, like name, address or phone, goes into the right drawer on the other side. Tricky lines, like names with several parts, come with extra rules.

sections.title: Keeping What Has No Registered Home: vCardProps, vCardParams, vCardName
sections.content:
A vCard may carry properties or parameters that have no IANA-registered JSContact property, such as extension elements an implementation does not understand. Three new JSContact properties let them survive conversion. Implementations MAY convert differently if they think that is more appropriate.

  • vCardProps (on a Card) is an array of JCardProp values, each a jCard-encoded vCard property as in RFC 7095.
  • vCardParams (on any object) is a JSON object of vCard parameters set on the property that produced the object.
  • vCardName (on any object) is the name of the vCard element that produced it, for example so that IMPP can be told apart from SOCIALPROFILE, since both become an OnlineService.

Properties with no registered counterpart, such as XML, GENDER, CLIENTPIDMAP and VERSION, are also meant to go through vCardProps. The vCard GENDER property can alternatively be expressed with the Card's speakToAs property.
sections.plainLanguage: If a card has a note that nobody understands, the guide says to tuck it into a labeled envelope and carry it along, so it can be handed back later.

sections.title: Converting JSContact to vCard
sections.content:
A Card converts to vCard by applying the reverse of the vCard-to-JSContact rules, which Appendix A lists for each JSContact type and property. Multivalued JSContact properties become separate instances of the equivalent vCard property, and each PROP-ID parameter MUST be set to the Id key of the converted value.

One mismatch needs a rule. The Name's full is optional in JSContact but FN is mandatory in vCard. If full is set, implementations MUST use it for FN. If not, they SHOULD derive a full name from the components. This can be done by concatenating the component values when isOrdered is true, or by another heuristic such as the Unicode CLDR person-name rules. The DERIVED parameter MUST be set on that FN. Otherwise FN MUST be set to the empty value.

Vendor-specific and unknown JSContact properties are converted with the new JSPROP property and JSPTR parameter, again with the freedom to convert differently if that seems more appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: Going the other way, the guide says to fill in every required box on the vCard. If a name box would be empty, build one from the parts and mark it as 'made up by a program'.

sections.title: JSPROP, JSPTR and JSCOMPS
sections.content:
JSPROP represents an arbitrary JSContact property in vCard. Its value is the JSON-encoded value as TEXT, in compact form without insignificant whitespace. It can occur several times, and the JSPTR parameter MUST be set on it. JSPTR holds a JSON pointer (RFC 6901) to the property inside the Card. The root is always the Card, the pointer MUST NOT reference into an array, and the value must be quoted because paths can contain a colon. All JSPROP properties together form a PatchObject, which MUST be applied only after all other vCard properties have been converted, and an invalid PatchObject MUST NOT be applied.

JSCOMPS preserves the order and separators of name and address components. The first entry is the default separator. The rest are either a position in the vCard structured value (an index, optionally followed by a comma and a second index) or a separator entry that starts with s,. When JSCOMPS is set and valid, the Name or Address isOrdered property MUST be true. When it is absent, isOrdered is false and defaultSeparator MUST NOT be set. It is valid only if every index exists and the count of positional entries equals the count of deduplicated component values.
sections.plainLanguage: JSPROP is a sticky note that says 'keep this odd detail exactly as written, and here is where it belongs'. JSCOMPS remembers the order words were written in, such as first name before last name.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The security section is short. It says this specification only defines conversion, and the security considerations for parsing and formatting such data apply, as outlined in Section 4 of RFC 9553 and Section 9 of RFC 6350.

IANA has added the vCard property JSPROP and the vCard parameter JSPTR to the vCard registries. It has also added the JSContact properties vCardName, vCardParams and vCardProps and the JSContact type JCardProp. For the JSContact entries, the Since Version is 1.0 and the Change Controller is IETF.
sections.plainLanguage: Translating a card does not add new dangers, so the guide just points to the safety rules the two card formats already have. New names for the new tools are written in the official lists.
